curriculum.title: Inner Break Stops Only the Inner Loop
curriculum.answer:
## Why inner `break` surprises you

You expected one `break` to stop everything. Python stops only the nearest loop [hub-cs50-loops-0015]. The outer loop still finishes its remaining values.

## Tiny runnable setup

Name two small lists. The outer variable selects a team; the inner variable selects an item. The names matter: a loop variable holds the current list item, not an index number.

```python
teams = ["red", "blue"]
items = ["a", "b"]
found = "none"
for t in teams:
    for v in items:
        if t == "red" and v == "a":
            found = "red-a"
            break
    print(t)
print(found)
```

The printed result is `red`, then `blue`, then `red-a`. The inner `break` ran when `t` was `"red"` and `v` was `"a"`.

## Where control goes next

`break` resumes immediately after the nearest enclosing loop [hub-cs50-loops-0015]. Here that means after the `for v in items:` loop, still inside the outer body. So `print(t)` still runs for `"red"`. Only then does the outer loop advance to `"blue"`. This outer-body-after-inner-loop pattern is normal in nested iteration [hub-cs50-loops-0039].

## Common wrong model

Wrong: “`break` escaped both loops, so `blue` never appears.” Right: “`break` escaped only the `v` loop, so the `t` loop continues.” Loop-`else` rules also depend on whether `break` occurred [hub-python-control-flow-0008], but we do not need them here.

## Added practice example

Change the first list to `["red", "blue", "green"]`. Predict the three team names that print. Then change the inner test so it never matches. Notice the same outer names still print; only the amount of inner work changes. Functions package this kind of test cleanly [hub-python-control-flow-0011].
